headline: Monopoly was invented to warn against monopolies

portrait.alt: Photograph of Lizzie Magie in profile, with short curly hair and a pale draped top
portrait.credit: Lizzie Magie, about 1892. Unknown photographer. Public domain.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: A lesson you could play
slides.text: Lizzie Magie followed Henry George, who argued that rent enriches landowners and keeps tenants poor. **She built a board game to show it.**
slides.alt: Studio portrait of the economist Henry George, balding, with a full beard and a bow tie
slides.credit: Henry George, about 1886. Unknown photographer. New York Public Library. Public domain.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: Patented and passed around
slides.text: She patented it on January 5, 1904, and players drew their own boards. **A Wharton economist taught with it in class.**
slides.alt: Patent drawing of a square game board with spaces marked For Sale and For Rent, railroads, a Bank, a Public Treasury and a Go to Jail corner
slides.credit: The Landlord's Game, US patent 748,626, 1904. Lizzie J. Magie. Public domain.

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: Monopoly
slides.statLabel: Monopoly sets sold worldwide, Hasbro said in 2015
slides.text: In 1935 Parker Brothers began selling a version called Monopoly. Its object: become the wealthiest player. **The warning became the goal.**

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: Her own rules pointed the way
slides.text: Her 1904 patent made getting rich the object, and the lesson relied on players noticing the cost. **A store version without the argument was harder to foresee.**

slides.label: The long cleanup
slides.title: Her name came back
slides.text: Parker Brothers paid her $500 for a revised patent in 1935, and by 1936 she was largely forgotten. **Research for a 1970s lawsuit brought her patents back.**

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: 275 million Monopoly sets sold, Hasbro said in 2015
A board still in use, with a jail and a corner to start from (US patent 748,626)
A game economics teachers used in class
costs: A game against land monopoly, best known for winning one
$500 for her patent, and decades without credit
Her anti-monopolist rules, largely forgotten by 1936
slides.text: It gave a board families still play, with 275 million sets sold by Hasbro's count. **It cost the lesson it was built to teach.**

slides.label: Pattern
slides.title: The lesson flipped
slides.text: To show the harm of land-grabbing, the game made land-grabbing the way to win. Players practiced it, and **the warning did not come in the box.**

slides.label: Lesson
slides.title: What we take from it
slides.text: People learn what they practice, not what they are told it means. **Put the lesson in the rules, not the commentary.**
